prompt.context: Our client, Harrison Energy, is one of the largest power & utilities companies in the US. You are in the year 2018, and the CEO sees electric vehicles as an attractive market and wants to enter the space. She needs help understanding how and when to enter the market, and the associated ROI. She has hired your firm to help formulate a strategy.
prompt.question: Help Harrison Energy formulate an EV market entry strategy: (1) What factors will you consider? (2) When should they enter the market? (3) Which parts of the EV value chain should they enter and how? (4) What other considerations should they prioritize?

clarifying_info.q: What is the goal of entering the EV market?
clarifying_info.a: The goal is to be present in a new market and add more sources of revenue and eventually profits.

clarifying_info.q: Is this limited to a specific geography?
clarifying_info.a: Scope is limited to the US market only.

clarifying_info.q: Is Harrison Energy currently in the EV market?
clarifying_info.a: No, the client is not currently involved in the EV market.

clarifying_info.q: Where in the EV value chain does Harrison Energy want to play?
clarifying_info.a: Harrison Energy does not yet know where in the EV value chain it wants to play.

clarifying_info.q: What is the target payback period for any investment?
clarifying_info.a: Harrison Energy wants to break-even on any investment within 5 years.

exhibits.title: Market Maturity and Total Cost of Ownership
exhibits.shows: Two charts: (1) EV Market Maturity Curve showing Introduction, Growth, Maturity, and Saturation phases from 2010 to 2050. (2) Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) for 10 years comparing EV components (Vehicles, Batteries, Maintenance, Electricity) vs ICE Vehicle, plotted from 2010 to 2050. Also includes a Price (TCO) to demand correlation chart showing demand at $40,000–$50,000 price range corresponding to 2,000,000–4,000,000 vehicles.

exhibits.title: Harrison Energy Capability Analysis
exhibits.shows: A matrix showing each EV value chain element (Vehicles, Batteries, Charging Stations, Power Generation, Software/Mgmt Services) across three value chain activities (Build, Sell, Operate). For each cell: market size in 2023 ($B), Harrison Energy's current capability level, time to build in-house, and cost to build in-house.

data.note: Assume best-case: 10% market share, 10% EBITDA margins. 5-year payback required.
data.capability_levels: Vehicles Build=15yr/$30B, Vehicles Sell=10yr/$5B, Vehicles Operate=10yr/$1B; Batteries Build=10yr/$600M, Batteries Sell=2yr/$50M, Batteries Operate=4yr/$100M; ChargingStations Build=2yr/$500M, ChargingStations Sell=Capable/$0, ChargingStations Operate=3yr/$300M; PowerGeneration Build=N/A, PowerGeneration Sell=Capable/$0, PowerGeneration Operate=Capable/$0; Software Build=1yr/$300M, Software Sell=Capable/$0, Software Operate=1yr/$200M

exhibits.title: Options for Acquisition
exhibits.shows: A table listing acquisition options for non-capable value chain elements, showing Component, Value Chain activity, Brand Alignment (Low/Medium/High), Option 1 (cheaper: Cost and Time), and Option 2 (faster: Cost and Time).

data.note: Same assumptions: 10% market share, 10% EBITDA margins, 5-year payback.

framework: Market: market size across EV components, growth rate, maturity of EV market (is tech still developing?), competitors and market share, regulations/policies in EV space
Financials: potential revenue (market size × share), potential costs (setup and operations)
Proposition: value chain components of EV, synergies with current business, customer segments (individual vs. business owners), supplier concentration
Entry strategy (per value chain element): M&A of smaller players vs. build from scratch (in-house or outsourced)

questions.prompt: When should Harrison Energy enter the EV market?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify both internal readiness (capabilities developed, capital raised) and external readiness (EV TCO < ICE TCO, adequate infrastructure, market in growth phase). External readiness is the binding constraint. Candidate should use Exhibit 1 to calculate the crossover year when EV TCO equals ICE TCO, using linear interpolation between 2020 and 2030 data points. Entry should coincide with the growth phase on the maturity curve.

math.setup: EV TCO in 2020 = $92,500; EV TCO in 2030 = $85,000; ICE TCO = $90,000. Find year when EV TCO = $90,000 using linear interpolation.
math.answer: EV TCO equals ICE TCO in 2023 — demand spikes at this point. 2023 is 5 years from 2018, aligning with the 5-year payback target. On the maturity curve, 2023 falls in the growth phase, the ideal entry window for a large company.

questions.prompt: Which parts of the EV value chain should Harrison Energy enter, and how?
questions.guidance: Candidate should: (1) Calculate expected annual profits per value chain element (market size × 10% share × 10% EBITDA); (2) Derive budget = expected profit × 5 (payback period); (3) Filter for elements where capability can be built in ≤5 years (by 2023); (4) Choose mode of entry (build in-house vs. Acquire Option 1 or 2) within budget; (5) Exclude Vehicles due to poor brand alignment and costs exceeding budget. Candidate should recognize that Batteries – Build slightly exceeds budget ($550M vs $500M) but is worth considering for a holistic batteries offering.

math.setup: For each value chain element: Expected Profit = Market Size × 10% × 10%. Budget = Expected Profit × 5. Filter: cost of entry ≤ budget AND time ≤ 5 years.
steps: Vehicles Build: $400B × 1% = $4B profit; budget $20B; cheapest ≤5yr option = Acquire Op#2 $40B → exceeds budget, brand alignment Low → NO
Vehicles Sell: $80B × 1% = $800M profit; budget $4B; no option ≤5yr → NO
Vehicles Operate: $25B × 1% = $250M profit; budget $1.25B; Acquire Op#2 $1.2B/5yr → fits budget but brand alignment Low → NO
Batteries Build: $10B × 1% = $100M profit; budget $500M; Acquire Op#2 $550M/5yr → slightly over budget, brand Medium → YES (holistic service)
Batteries Sell: $3B × 1% = $30M profit; budget $150M; Build $50M/2yr → YES
Batteries Operate: $3B × 1% = $30M profit; budget $150M; Build $100M/4yr → YES
Charging Stations Build: $12B × 1% = $120M profit; budget $600M; Acquire Op#1 $400M/4yr → YES
Charging Stations Sell: $2B × 1% = $20M profit; budget $100M; Already Capable/$0 → YES
Charging Stations Operate: $5B × 1% = $50M profit; budget $250M; Already Capable/$0 → YES
Power Generation Sell: $10B × 1% = $100M profit; budget $500M; Already Capable/$0 → YES
Power Generation Operate: $4B × 1% = $40M profit; budget $200M; Already Capable/$0 → YES
Software Build: $3B × 1% = $30M profit; budget $150M; Acquire Op#1 $100M/3yr → YES
Software Operate: $3B × 1% = $30M profit; budget $150M; Acquire Op#1 $100M/3yr → YES
Total for Yes entries: ~$550M expected annual profit; ~$1,300M total investment cost
math.answer: Enter all value chains except Vehicles (poor brand alignment, costs exceed budget). Total expected annual profit ≈ $550M. Harrison already has capabilities in 5 elements; can build 2 in-house; acquires 6 (3 via Option 1, 3 via Option 2) within 5-year payback.

questions.prompt: What other considerations should Harrison Energy prioritize when entering the EV market?
questions.guidance: Strong answers identify customer segments, geographic prioritization, regulatory tailwinds, and competitive advantages. Top answers note that large utilities have structural advantages over pure-play competitors.

brainstorming.prompt: What other considerations should Harrison Energy have to prioritize market entry?

categories.name: Target Customer Segments
ideas: Pursue business/industrial customers electrifying fleets first (e.g., UPS, PepsiCo) before individual consumers
Fleet operators provide larger, more predictable revenue streams
Corporate sustainability mandates accelerate B2B demand

categories.name: Geographic Prioritization
ideas: Power & utility companies typically operate as regulated monopolies in specific states
Enter own operating states first to leverage existing customer relationships and infrastructure
Expand to adjacent states once initial model is proven

categories.name: Regulations & Government
ideas: Tax incentives and rebates encouraging EV adoption lower consumer cost barriers
Government sustainability programs can be leveraged for favorable treatment
Harrison's existing government relationships give an advantage in navigating regulatory approvals

categories.name: Competitive Advantages over Specialized Players
ideas: Established customer base reduces marketing costs
Existing manufacturing and distribution networks enable easier scaling
Better supplier relations increase bargaining power
Deeper understanding of customer energy usage enables more targeted propositions
Stronger government relations to leverage EV incentives

recommendation: Harrison Energy should enter the EV market in approximately 2023 (5 years from 2018), when EV Total Cost of Ownership falls below that of ICE vehicles and demand spikes, coinciding with the growth phase of the market maturity curve.

Harrison should enter all EV value chain segments except Vehicles due to poor ROI and poor brand alignment. Expected annual profit from selected segments is approximately $550M (in 2023 dollars). Harrison already has existing capabilities in 5 elements; it should build 2 in-house and acquire competitors in 6 segments (3 via cheaper Option 1, 3 via faster Option 2), all within the 5-year payback period constraint.
risks: Outsourcing and acquisitions may not yield the capabilities needed for further innovation, limiting long-term competitiveness
Suppliers and acquisition targets may have high bargaining power, resulting in longer timelines and higher costs than modeled
Overlooking Vehicles — the largest value chain element — may cede significant future market share if brand alignment issues can be overcome
next_steps: Start negotiations with suppliers and acquisition targets immediately
Identify specific customer segments (e.g., fleet operators) to pilot existing capabilities in Power Generation, Charging Stations, and Software
Create a new organizational structure or hire specialized consultants to execute the EV market entry project
